accuracy.evidence: Facts checked against named sources: sleep after learning helps consolidate new memories, with slow-wave sleep replaying the day's learning (Diekelmann and Born 2010, Nature Reviews Neuroscience; Rasch and Born 2013, Physiological Reviews); children benefit at least as much as adults (Wilhelm et al. 2013, Nature Neuroscience); about one hour less sleep a night for three nights worsened 9 to 12 year olds' attention and memory measures (Sadeh, Gruber and Raviv 2003, Child Development); 9 to 12 hours for ages 6 to 12 (Paruthi et al. 2016, AASM consensus); no screens in the hour before bed (NHS sleep advice for children). The lab's memory shelf is labelled in the adult text and the lab header as a picture of the idea, not a measurement. Clock sums verified: 8:30 pm to 7:00 am is 10 and a half hours, 10:30 pm to 7:00 am is 8 and a half; parameterised items checked at the corners: n+7 gives 9 to 12 (p2), n-k gives 7 to 10 (p4), nk gives 18 to 44 (m6), n+60 gives 70 to 90 (m8).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the slips adults see in children this age: the brain switches off at night (prediction 1, p1, challenge), more late practice of the same page beats sleep (prediction 2 and the Ava and Ben night, p3, the 'late' refusal), sleep as wasted study time (sort card, m1, challenge), sleep replacing practice (p5, challenge 'Yes, sleep teaches you new things'), counting forward instead of back for a bedtime or accepting 11:00 pm for a 7:00 am wake (prediction 3, the bedtime rail refusals with the hour count, m3, challenge), and a screen or game right at lights out (prediction 4, the 8:00 pm and 9:00 pm tablet refusals, m5).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagsleepmem is built on this topic's own mechanism: a moon dragged across a night sky that moves the day's practice from a desk to a memory shelf while the child sleeps; the same moon run over two lanes where Ben stays awake until 10:30 pm and his shelf fills later; a bedtime rail from 6 pm to midnight where the hours of sleep are counted back from three different wake times and checked against 9 to 12; a habits sort; and an evening timeline with fixed dinner, bath and lights out where a tablet game is refused in the last hour. It differs from 491 flagsleep (teen body clock, social jet lag, caffeine) and 424 eating, sleeping and moving; the lab-distinct gate passed against every flag lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers before being told: dragging the moon makes each practised item jump to the shelf at a named time ('1:00 am: asleep, your brain stores spell: because'); the two-lane night shows Ben still awake while Ava's shelf fills ('11:00 pm: Ava has stored 1, Ben has stored 0') and ends with 10 and a half against 8 and a half hours; dragging the bed to 11:00 pm for a 7:00 am wake is refused with 'only 8 hours' and the count-back hint; the tablet game dropped on 8:00 pm is refused with the screen-free hour, while 7:00 pm is accepted. Real mouse drags at 390 px confirmed each message.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 'When you are asleep, is your brain switched off?' (Yes, it rests; the shelf fills during the night), 'Who will remember more spellings tomorrow?' (Ben: he practised for longer; the two-lane night shows Ava storing more), 'You wake at 7:00 am. Is going to bed at 11:00 pm enough sleep?' (Yes, that is plenty; the rail shows 8 hours and refuses it), 'A tablet game ends right at lights out. Will you fall asleep just as fast?' (Yes, games make you sleepy; the plan refuses screens in the last hour).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions with a separate message per wrong answer: 'Yes, it rests and does nothing' gets 'Your brain is busy at night', 'Do one more hour of the same tables' gets 'Doing the same page again late at night cuts your sleep', '10:00 pm' for a 10-hour night gets 'Count back 10 hours from 7:00 am: 10:00 pm gives only 9 hours', '11:00 pm' gets 'only 8 hours', 'Do not practise, just sleep' gets 'Sleep stores practice. It does not replace it', and 'He will fall asleep faster' gets the screen message. Answer order rotates per question.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and concrete words (practise, sleep, store, count back, tablet) and pass the learner readability limit in learn/validate_lessons.py; the adult text passes the adult limit. Canvas labels are short (Today's desk, Memory shelf, Wake up at 7:00 am, Lights out); every feedback line is one or two sentences naming the fix.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate clean (no filler phrases). Each kid paragraph adds one idea: the brain works at night; Ava and Ben; how many hours and how to count back; practise first, screens off, morning check. Adult paragraphs give the research basis with named studies, the hours guidance and how the lab turns it into steps, the common mistakes with the honest caveat about the shelf model, and how the lesson differs from the other two sleep lessons.

mobile.evidence: Checked 390 px screenshots before and after Show me for all five scenes, plus 1200 px desktop in dark theme: night sky track with end labels that no longer collide with the moving clock label, bed and desk-and-shelf columns; two lanes with five shelf slots each and a one-line result; a bedtime rail with hour labels, a 'Bed' marker and a large wake-time card; eight habit cards in a 2 x 4 grid over two trays; and eight timeline rows beside four job cards. Real drags at 390 px worked for the moon, the bed marker, card to tray and job to time.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: 'Moon on 2 hours' and 'To morning' for the night scenes, Earlier, Later and Set bedtime for the rail, Helps and Gets in the way buttons per habit with full-sentence aria-labels, and one button per job per free time in the plan. The canvas aria-label carries the instructions, each stored item, the lane counts, every refusal and the challenge question; challenge feedback is a role=status live region; ticks, crosses and counts mark state as well as colour. The browser gate runs axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
